steps.why: The definition needs three words, not one: the small molecule, the large molecule, and the joining. Naming the monomer and the polymer separately is what makes the definition usable on any example a question supplies.
common_mistakes: Calling the small molecule the polymer. The small starting molecule is the monomer.
Saying the molecules are simply mixed. They are joined by chemical bonds into one molecule.
Leaving out the word many. One or two molecules joining is not a polymerisation.
steps.memory_tip: Many monomers join into one polymer; poly means many.
steps.margin_note: Define both words, monomer and polymer, then attach one example.

steps.label: The example
lines: Ethylene is the monomer and polythene is
1500–2000 atm with a trace of oxygen.
ethylene molecule with its double bond
steps.why: Ethylene to polythene shows the whole definition in one line: the monomer on the left, the polymer on the right, and the repeating unit visible inside the bracket. The double bond opening is what supplies the two bonds that join each unit to its neighbours.
common_mistakes: Keeping the double bond in the product. Every double bond opens as the chain forms.
Leaving out the n. The n says that many monomer units are joined, which is the point of the definition.
steps.memory_tip: The double bond opens on every molecule, and the opened units link into a chain.
steps.margin_note: Write the n on both sides and name the monomer and the polymer.
